title: The Disappearing Student Safety Net
summary:
The Disappearing Student Safety Net
Joshua.Bay Tue, 07/28/2026 - 03:00 AM

New analysis from the Hope Center found that even though more colleges are offering aid for emergencies, awareness gaps and limited funding mean fewer students are receiving support.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
An unexpected expense is one of the most common reasons students stop out of college. Research has showed that emergency aid—a timely grant that helps students cover unexpected costs—can greatly improve the odds that they stay enrolled and complete a degree or credential.

However, a new analysis from the Hope Center for Student Basic Needs at Temple University found that despite growth in emergency aid programs on college campuses, far fewer students are receiving that assistance.

The analysis is based on data from Trellis Strategies’ most recent Student Financial Wellness Survey of more than 65,000 undergraduate students across 153 institutions nationwide. It found that the share of students receiving emergency aid fell from 44 percent in fall 2021 to 4 percent in fall 2025—a decline of roughly 90 percent.

Muhammad Kara, policy and research analyst at the center, said emergency aid is designed to help students respond quickly to an unforeseen financial crisis. Unlike traditional financial aid, which is packaged months before a term and disbursed on a fixed schedule, he said, emergency aid can be distributed when a student faces an immediate expense.

Kara said the decline in students receiving emergency aid suggests colleges are either failing to publicize available support or operating programs that are too limited in scope or funding to meet student need.

“These have real-world applications,” Kara said. “If a student can’t pay a medical bill or afford food or housing, they’re really not going to be focused on their academics.”

The awareness gap: The report found that the share of institutions offering emergency aid has increased over the same period. According to survey research from the National Association of Student Financial Aid Administrators, the percentage of member institutions operating an emergency aid program rose from 35 percent in 2020 to 52 percent in 2025.

But federal data reveals a disconnect between program growth and student awareness. The Beginning Postsecondary Students Longitudinal Study, which tracked students who first enrolled in 2019–20 and were still enrolled in 2022, found that only about one-quarter of students reported that their institution offered emergency aid, while more than two-thirds said they did not know whether such aid was available.

The findings reflect a broader awareness gap among college students. Inside Higher Ed’s most recent Student Voice survey of 5,065 students from 260 two- and four-year institutions found that 64 percent of respondents did not know if their institution offered such assistance.

Kara said that gap between institutional supply and student awareness raises an uncomfortable possibility: that some colleges may be quietly declining to publicize their emergency aid because they don’t think they can afford the demand that greater awareness would generate.

“Some students may apply for it, but that expense is so near and dear, and it’s so evident at that present moment that even if they apply, they won’t get it within the timeliness aspect,” Kara said. “So they may have missed that, or just didn’t really get it when they absolutely needed it.”

The consequences can be significant, he said, because many students lack the financial cushion to absorb even a relatively small unexpected expense.

“Most students don’t have enough savings to cover a $500 bill. That could be a medical bill, a car repair, and there are a lot of students leaning on riskier ways of borrowing like credit cards or predatory loans,” Kara said. “That makes us worried in the basic needs space because we’re trying to figure out innovative financial ways for students to meet those needs.”

A patchwork response: During the pandemic, Congress provided nearly $40 billion in emergency aid to students through the Higher Education Emergency Relief Fund. However, the report notes, only seven states now have dedicated state-level emergency aid programs, which collectively provide roughly $46 million annually—about 0.1 percent of the expired federal investment.

Kara argued that federal emergency aid worked and that Congress could expand access to such aid without additional spending by allowing colleges to once again use Federal Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grant funds as emergency grants. He warned that without this flexibility, more students may continue to struggle with unexpected expenses that can derail their education.

“If this flexibility isn’t granted and/or if the funding is reduced, more students are going to continue to struggle,” Kara said. “Students are going to continue to turn to more risky financial avenues, which doesn’t help students succeed and does not help their financial health whatsoever.”

He said that in the interim, institutions should look for ways to invest in emergency assistance programs for students facing financial challenges.

“What universities can do is definitely invest in some form of emergency assistance, emergency aid, for those students,” Kara said. “I know those are easier said than done, and I know most universities are strapped when it comes to state appropriations and just funding in general. But if we are seeing a subset of students who really need $500, in the bigger scheme of things, $500 is not a lot.”

title: Compton College Plans to Tie Basic Needs to Academic Milestones. Will It Work?
summary:
Compton College Plans to Tie Basic Needs to Academic Milestones. Will It Work?
Sara Weissman Tue, 07/28/2026 - 03:00 AM

Starting in fall 2027, students need to meet a set of academic requirements to get free meals and other supports. College leaders say the move will increase completion rates. But basic needs experts are worried.

Byline(s)
Sara Weissman
full_text:
For years, Compton College has been a forerunner in the push for basic needs support for its students. The community college in Los Angeles offers students one free meal per day, in addition to transit passes, food pantry access and weekly $20 vouchers for its on-campus farmers market. It also has a unique data-sharing agreement with the Los Angeles Department of Public and Social Services to help students sign up for food benefits, and the college plans to open the first community college student housing in L.A. next summer.

Those services were born out of high need: A 2025 #RealCollege survey found that more than half of respondents from the college reported facing food insecurity in the last 30 days. A whopping 68 percent said they’d experienced housing insecurity in the last year.

But some supports for those students will soon have strings attached. Starting in fall 2027, Compton is launching a controversial new plan that ties some basic needs supports to academic requirements, in the hopes of upping completion rates at the college. Compton leaders say the goal is to incentivize students to take steps toward completion, graduate them more quickly and reduce the number of students reliant on these resources year to year, making it easier for the college to continue to afford providing services to other students. But some basic needs experts worry the move will deter financially strapped students from accessing food supports.

Under the new plan, students starting their second year will only be able to access free meals and farmers market vouchers if they complete a set of tasks, including filing an education plan and signing up for Handshake, a career-preparation platform, by the end of their first year. Degree-seeking or transfer students will need to take transfer-level English and math in their first year of enrollment and pass those courses by the end of their third year. They will also need to earn credits at a steady clip—at least nine units per semester—but they can’t accumulate too many credits, either. Depending on their major, students have a cap of 70 or 80 units before they lose access to supports. The move is intended to encourage students to stay on track and avoid taking extra credits they don’t need to transfer or graduate. Certificate students and noncredit students have their own sets of requirements, and dual-enrollment students are exempt.

Some supports, such as the food pantry, transit passes and technology loans will remain open to all students—as long as they’re in good financial standing with the college.

Compton College President Keith Curry sees the policy shift as one step toward the larger goal of ratcheting up student completion rates by 2035, a charge from the California Community Colleges system to its institutions. He said a deep dive into the college’s data shows too many students are racking up excess credits without graduating or transferring, or they’re not taking or passing the classes they need to transfer, sometimes spending down their Pell Grants and hurting their ability to afford future education.

He emphasized that educational plans, and other measures on the list of requirements, have been shown to improve completion rates, but getting students to fulfill them—even when they’re mandatory—can be a challenge.

“If a student doesn’t have an ed plan, doesn’t go see a counselor … the counselors are going to classrooms, they’re doing everything they’re supposed to do, but the students are not coming in … what do you want me to do?” he said.

Fewer than a third, 27 percent, of Compton College students graduate, and 10 percent transfer out, within three years, according to 2024 data from the Department of Education’s Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System. Compton’s most recent strategic plan promises to tackle completion rates, and the college also committed to increasing a range of student success outcomes—like course success, persistence and completion rates for transfer-level English and math—by 2035. The basic needs strategy is one piece of that work, according to Curry.

“It’s about institutional transformation,” Curry said. “We’re setting expectations for our students because … that’s how important it is that we want to see our students complete.”

Curry also wants the college to keep up the level of basic needs services it currently offers, but it’s “not sustainable” if students are staying enrolled for “five to six or seven years” and straining those services, he said. For the past academic year, as of March, the college spent $186,000 on technology support, $326,000 on food services and over $62,000 on housing support. More than 5,500 students got free meals through Everytable, a company that partners with the college to combat food insecurity, and 851 students got farmers market vouchers.

The college plans to share the new basic needs requirements with students next month.

“We’re messaging it to students, ‘This is about helping to support you,’” Curry said. “But my gut and what I feel is—and I’ve seen this before in our community—students are going to step up to the expectation because they have seen the institution step up for them.”

Strong Reactions

Basic needs experts, however, are leery. They argue the plan would put up extra barriers for students and deter them from accessing the college’s resources.

Nicholas Freudenberg, Distinguished Professor of public health emeritus at the City University of New York, who led work on the CUNY system’s food insecurity program, said he’s all for keeping students on track, but he worries that tying otherwise positive academic requirements to students’ food supports will backfire and hurt students.

“Everything I know about both public benefits and college benefits is that the more requirements you add, the more you lose people, and often the people you lose are the neediest people,” he said.

He emphasized that many community college students struggle with “time poverty” as they juggle work, family care and other responsibilities, making it harder for them to figure out—much less complete—new requirements.

“They just have so much to do to get through their daily lives, and to add new requirements seems at best pointless and at worst cruel,” Freudenberg said. He also worries the students best able to access Compton’s free meals and other services may be the students with the most bandwidth to meet the new standards, not necessarily those who most need the supports.

Mark Huelsman, director of policy and advocacy at the Hope Center, said even requiring students be in good financial standing with the college to access technology loans or the food pantry could block students from services they need. He said students can fall into a vicious cycle where financial precarity puts them behind on payments to the college, limiting their access to food and other benefits that could help them get into a better financial situation. He fears “penalizing students if they get tripped up financially.”

“Where we want to be extremely careful with these kinds of things is making sure that students aren’t faced with undue red tape or administrative burdens or other hurdles just to be able to eat at the end of the day,” Huelsman said.

He noted that Compton’s approach is reminiscent of some campus and state emergency aid programs, as well as the federal financial aid system, which require students to maintain satisfactory academic performance to access or retain benefits.

He emphasized that the requirements Compton is putting in place do help students to complete—but so do basic needs supports, and he worries about pitting one against the other.

“Integrating basic needs supports into broader completion strategies is a great concept,” he said, citing as an example the practice of connecting students using food and housing services to academic supports like career counseling. “I think the devil’s in the details.”

Huelsman also sympathized with community college leaders like Compton, who are trying to offer a wide range of benefits “with less than ideal funding,” especially as cuts to federal benefit programs like the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and Medicaid put more pressure on campuses to fill the gaps.

But he doesn’t want savings to come from students not taking advantage of services that could help them, he said. The question is, “Are you saving money because students are … getting to and through faster, or are you saving money because fewer students are even seeking help in the first place?”

A Test Case

Others support experimenting with hinging basic needs services on steps toward college completion.

Meacie Fairfax, strategy director at Complete College America, praised Compton for taking an innovative approach.

“Compton College does deserve real credit for trying to link basic needs to completion outcomes rather than just treating them as separate efforts,” she said. “We want to make sure that [students] get to those milestones.”

She has some concerns about students’ access to supports, but said the requirements are designed to kick in after a student’s first year, which gives them some time to learn what services are available and what’s expected of them.

She also said it makes sense that colleges that invest large sums in student services and supports want to ensure “we and they are getting a return on the investments that they’re putting into our colleges.”

Over all, she believes the requirements align with research on college completion, and she’s curious to see what Compton learns.

“This is the kind of experimentation that the field needs,” she said of Compton’s plan, “and we welcome it as long as it comes back with … some information to inform the field. They’re leaning in the right direction, because these are things that are actually only going to be beneficial for these students.”

Curry said he expected a range of reactions. His own faculty members responded to the idea with a mix of concern and support. But he nonetheless believes the new strategy is “groundbreaking” and potentially a model for other colleges to follow. He also emphasized that the college is going to monitor how the policy affects students every year.

“Will some of these advocates say, ‘Oh, I don’t know about this’?” he said. “Yeah, but … we have to continue to focus on completion, because in higher ed, we’re going to be criticized for return on investment and economic mobility of our students. That means we have to make sure our students complete in a timely manner, make sure our students transfer or get a job when they leave our institutions.”

title: Some parents on benefits to get up to £4,500 for child starting apprenticeship
summary: Some parents on benefits lose income if their children take on apprenticeships.
full_text:
Some parents on benefits will be given up to £4,500 a year to encourage their children to start apprenticeships, the government has said.

Under plans to encourage young people into work, families will be offered a bursary to replace Universal Credit payments lost by starting jobs.

The payment is expected to benefit an estimated few thousand households, who currently face losing between £17 and £330 a week if their children start apprenticeships.

The Conservatives welcomed Prime Minister Andy Burnham's support for apprenticeships, but criticised his plans to fund the bursaries.

The bursary will be paid for from a £30m pot, funded through the growth and skills levy, a tax on employers with annual wage bills over £3m.

It followed the publication of a Social Security Advisory Committee report, external which warned of the "perverse effects" of the benefits system on young people's employment choices.

It said, for example, single parents with a disabled child could lose up to £340 per week in benefits if their child started an apprenticeship, exceeding the expected apprenticeship salary of £258 per week.

Because they are classed as paid employment, benefit payments are reduced to households where young people take on apprenticeships.

The committee said the system was hampering government efforts to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet).

In a recent report, former Health Secretary Alan Milburn warned that one in six young people could be Neet in the next five years unless urgent action is taken.

Official figures show more than a million people aged 16 to 24 are currently Neet.

The government said its new bursary would remove a barrier to young people taking on apprenticeships, allowing them to "earn and learn".

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said: "By providing bursaries to those who need them most and fully funding apprenticeship training, we are making sure cost is not the reason someone misses out."

It is part of a wider package of support for apprenticeships, including funding for apprenticeship training for under-25s and additional support for employers taking on apprentices.

Helen Whately, the Shadow Work and Pensions Secretary, said: "I'm glad Burnham agrees: apprenticeships are a good thing, and we need more of them."

But she said the plan was "uncosted".

"It is spending money already committed elsewhere. So, either it is another unfunded announcement, or Andy Burnham is not being straight with us about his plans."

Burnham has said he is "on a mission" to reduce the number of Neets.

"The trend is rising at the moment, so the first thing I've got to do is to stop that rise," he said.

As he continues a flurry of early policy announcements, Burnham on Tuesday set out plans to strike a balance in the education system between prioritising academic and technical skills.

title: 150 years of the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science
summary: The IACS has cultivated a legacy of intellectual curiosity, scientific excellence, and national service that continues to inspire generations of researchers, Shekhar Mande writes
full_text:
The late 18th and 19th centuries marked a period of profound intellectual and cultural awakening across India, with Bengal emerging as its prominent centre. Although similar currents of intellectual, social, and cultural reform were taking shape in several other parts of the country, the scale, diversity, and enduring influence of this awakening found their fullest expression in Bengal.

What is now widely known as the Bengal Renaissance not only transformed Bengal but also profoundly influenced the intellectual, social, and cultural evolution of modern India. The movement fostered remarkable advances across a broad spectrum of disciplines, ranging from philosophy, spirituality, literature, and the arts to education, social reform, and the natural sciences. It produced an extraordinary generation of philosophers, reformers, educators, scientists, writers, and artists whose collective vision and achievements laid many of the intellectual and institutional foundations of modern India.

One of the most influential figures of this remarkable period was Mahendralal Sircar (1833-1904). Deeply concerned that the colonial administration had failed to provide adequate opportunities for Indians to pursue education and research in the natural sciences, Sircar articulated a bold vision for scientific self-reliance.

In 1869, in an article published in the Calcutta Journal of Medicine, he proposed the establishment of the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science (IACS), arguing that scientific education was indispensable for India’s intellectual and societal progress. As he wrote: “The best method, and under the present circumstances, the only method, that we can conceive of, by which the people of India can be essentially improved, by which the Hindu mind can/ be developed to its full proportions, is as we have seen above, by the cultivation of the Physical Sciences”.

Three years later, while addressing a meeting of the Bethune Society at the Medical College Theatre in Calcutta in 1872, Sircar lamented the lack of institutional support for scientific research in India under colonial rule: “I must say, though I say with deep regret, that our Government has hitherto afforded no opportunity, nor offered any encouragement to the pursuit of science by the native of this country”.

These statements reveal Sircar’s remarkable foresight. At a time when scientific research in India received little official encouragement, he envisioned an institution that would enable Indians to pursue scientific inquiry and contribute to the advancement of knowledge. That vision culminated in the establishment of the IACS on July 29, 1876, as the country’s first national institution dedicated to scientific research by Indians. Today, as we celebrate its 150th anniversary, we honour not merely the founding of an institution but the birth of a scientific movement that transformed the landscape of Indian science.

Among the most celebrated scientists associated with the IACS was C.V. Raman, whose pioneering work transformed modern physics. Shortly after joining the Accountant General’s Office in Calcutta in 1907, Raman noticed a “strange-looking board” bearing the name ‘Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science’. Intrigued, he made enquiries about the institution and was introduced to Amrit Lal Sircar, the son of the Association’s founder. Recognising Raman’s enthusiasm for scientific research, Amrit extended an open invitation to use the Association’s laboratories for Raman’s experiments outside office hours.

For nearly a decade, Raman followed a remarkable routine. He spent the early mornings and evenings at the IACS laboratory while discharging his responsibilities as a government officer during the day. This extraordinary dedication continued until 1917, when he resigned from the Finance Department to accept the Palit Professorship of Physics at the University of Calcutta. Even thereafter, IACS remained the principal venue for his experimental investigations.

It was in the laboratories of IACS that Raman made his most celebrated discovery, the Raman effect, which he announced to the world on February 28, 1928. This landmark discovery earned him the Nobel Prize in physics in 1930, making him the first Asian scientist to win this prize in the sciences. In many ways, Raman’s achievement represented the fulfilment of Mahendralal Sircar’s vision: that an institution founded and nurtured by Indians for the cultivation of science could produce discoveries of the highest international significance.

The founding of the IACS also marked a defining moment in the renaissance of science in India. More than the establishment of a scientific institution, it embodied the aspiration that Indians should not merely learn science but actively create it. Over the past century and a half, IACS has nurtured generations of exceptional scientists, provided a vibrant institutional framework for the pursuit of scientific inquiry, and made contributions of enduring significance to the advancement of science worldwide.

As we commemorate this historic milestone, we pay our deepest tribute to the vision and foresight of Mahendralal Sircar, whose unwavering belief in the transformative power of science made this institution possible. We also celebrate the extraordinary legacy of the IACS itself, a legacy of intellectual curiosity, scientific excellence, and national service that continues to inspire generations of researchers. May that spirit continue to guide the Institute advancing the frontiers of knowledge and contributing to the scientific and technological progress of India and the world.

full_text:
Once upon a time, there was this brave professor, who opened a word processor app to develop one of their most important tools in life; the syllabus.

When we design courses, we are focused on sharing knowledge that will be both informational and contextual. For this we integrate objectives, activities, and for the more technical part, assessments, rubrics, and references that make up the traditional sense of learning. Time after time we have understood that this document is a syllabus. A syllabus, as I have heard and said in faculty meetings, is the contract that binds you with the student of what is going to happen during the term. Honestly, though reflecting on the topic of the syllabus, I don’t know where my courses would be heading if I didn’t use or follow a syllabus. Even following one, I sometimes drift within the wind.

But as I was reading Everyday Christian Teaching by Dr. David Smith, in the chapter titled Speaking, Hearing, Hospitality, in just the first paragraph he writes: “Teachers do not simply list course content for learners. They sequence it in ways that imply a story about what fits together and where it is headed.” (2025, p.73). Automatically I asked myself, what is the story my syllabus is telling students? To be completely honest, is it even telling a story at all?

Storytelling, according to the National Storytelling Association (n.d.) is the interactive art of using words and actions to reveal the elements and images of a story while encouraging the listener’s imagination. This definition prompts me to ask; are our syllabus helping students to foster their imagination? Are the taxonomies where including prompting a learning environment of freedom is designing experiences that can build stories, history, and legacy? Or are we limiting our syllabus to inform standardization and skillful citations of the authors we love and the topics we enjoy? Is your syllabus helping your students at all?

Connecting storytelling to syllabus preparation can be complex for our traditional learning settings. But if we were to transcend the traditional scope of our preparation process, the stories implied and exposed in the syllabus would make our disciplines less intimidating. If in an algebra course, the story would imply the adventure of problem based learning and solutions; if in a philosophy course, the story would be to vanquish the prejudice of life’s toughest questions; if in a business course, the story would present the transformation of a context to define day-to-day entrepreneurship; or in a theology course, the story would connect the divine intervention process, not as a Marvel movie but as a caring grandmother’s actions.

One interesting factor in defining characters and their roles in the syllabus process as a storytelling process, is to define who is the author, narrator, and readers. The author is the professor. You are the author, idealist, and architect of the story line. This is an important role because this is the connection and development of a story and its direct implications for students and imagining the impact of this content. As a reader, you probably remember an interesting book, article, or just a post on social media that captivativated your attention. Could we ask ourselves as professors if our syllabus captivates our student’s attention? In the case of the readers, they’re students. They adventure themselves into the topics and depths of the content we intended to teach them. They navigate that content with the tools and experiences they bring to contextualize and hopefully impact their present and future surroundings.

A neuralgic factor in the story of the syllabus is the Narrator. This is the subject or voice that defines the tone, context, and processes emotions into the changes of the story. In the case of our syllabus; who is the narrator? Whose voice is narrating the content of our course? This is an important part to reflect on.

Here are some questions that can help along that process: What theories? What authors? What dates and historical facts? Which exercises define the practical sense of our course? Who’s perspective is forming our readers’ experiences and the author’s input? Only men? Only women? Only white? Only a western or oriental mindset? The narrator in the storytelling process of the syllabus speaks of our own stories. It can capture our biases, preferences, and experiences (whether good or bad) and as educators we must be honest and aware to consider the voice that moves the teaching and learning process in our course.

The story of our courses develop with emotions, frictions, tensions, experiences, questions, and context; lots and lots of context. Here is a simple guide to help each other reframe the storytelling process of our syllabus, so our authorship can be balanced, our readers well informed, and our narrator intentional.

Preparing a syllabus to tell a story implies that:

The course description must set the tone for the overview of the story of your course.

The objectives must present characters, both literal and metaphorical, that will be present to guide the learning experience. As well as expose the solution that your students must overcome with the knowledge they will receive.

The topics are to present the settings, set backs, and how to manage the plot.

The assessments and requirements will serve as the voice of the story, where the professor and students will be guided to discern continuously to give life, action, and solution to the conflict, in the particular setting.

The references and institutional guidelines, instead of serving as page expansions, should serve as the relationship dynamic between all of the contexts and characters that will develop and wait for a solution.

The end.

Dr. Daniel Andrés Rivera Rosado is the Director of the JFU Bible Institute of La Iglesia Cristiana (Discípulos de Cristo) en Puerto Rico. He is also an adjunct faculty member of Christian Education at the Seminario Evangélico de Puerto Rico. He earned a PhD in Education from the University of Arizona Global Campus, researching the behavioral intention of technology integration in theological educators’ teaching practices. Daniel is the author of four books: Misión Activa: El quehacer del liderazgo en la Iglesia local (2022), El ABC de la Educación Cristiana (2023), Influencia Intencional: Liderazgo Educativo para el ministerio (2024) y Quietud: Otra manera de vivir la misión (2025).

Smith, D. (2025). Everyday Christian Teaching: A guide to practicing faith in the classroom. Grand Rapids; Eerdmans Publishing Co.

title: Under Pressure: Warum Digitale Souveränität zur Organisationsaufgabe wird
summary:
Im Juni haben wir im Rahmen des University:Future Festivals unter dem Motto „Under Pressure” gemeinsam gelernt, diskutiert und uns ausgetauscht. In verschiedenen Blogartikeln wollen wir nun auf die zentralen Themen zurückblicken, die das Festival in diesem Jahr besonders geprägt haben. Den Anfang macht heute Michael Siegel mit einem Rückblick auf die Veranstaltungen des Festivals, bei denen es um Digitale Souveränität ging.

The post Under Pressure: Warum Digitale Souveränität zur Organisationsaufgabe wird appeared first on Hochschulforum Digitalisierung.
full_text:
Im Juni haben wir im Rahmen des University:Future Festivals unter dem Motto „Under Pressure” gemeinsam gelernt, diskutiert und uns ausgetauscht. In verschiedenen Blogartikeln wollen wir nun auf die zentralen Themen zurückblicken, die das Festival in diesem Jahr besonders geprägt haben. Den Anfang macht heute Michael Siegel mit einem Rückblick auf die Veranstaltungen des Festivals, bei denen es um Digitale Souveränität ging.

Wie können Hochschulen ihre digitale Zukunft gestalten, ohne die Kontrolle über ihre Daten, Infrastrukturen und Entscheidungen zu verlieren? Beim University:Future Festival 2025 stand diese Frage vor allem im Zeichen wachsender Abhängigkeiten von großen Technologieunternehmen. Open Source erschien als Gegenentwurf zu Lock-ins, Blackboxes und dem Verlust institutioneller Gestaltungsspielräume.

Ein Jahr später hat sich die Lage weiter zugespitzt. Künstliche Intelligenz hält Einzug in Lehre, Forschung und Verwaltung, Kostenmodelle verändern sich, Sicherheitsanforderungen steigen – während Geld, Personal und Zeit knapp bleiben. Das Festivalmotto „Under Pressure“ beschrieb damit auch die Ausgangslage der Debatte über Digitale Souveränität.

Die Sessions des U:FF 2026 zeigten jedoch: Der Diskurs ist nicht bei der Warnung vor Abhängigkeiten stehen geblieben. Digitale Souveränität wird konkreter. Im Mittelpunkt steht zunehmend die Frage, wie Hochschulen unter realen Bedingungen handlungsfähig bleiben – und welche technischen, organisatorischen und finanziellen Strukturen sie dafür benötigen.

Nicht ob Hochschulen unter Druck stehen, sei die entscheidende Frage, sondern: Welche Form nehmen sie unter diesem Druck an?

Digitalisierung könne Lehre, Forschung und Zusammenarbeit unterstützen. Plattformisierung beginne dagegen dort, wo nicht mehr nur neue Werkzeuge eingesetzt werden, sondern deren Logik die Institution verändert: wenn Kennzahlen Urteile ersetzen, Skalierbarkeit zum Qualitätskriterium wird und Algorithmen darüber mitbestimmen, was sichtbar und wertvoll ist.

Digitale Souveränität betrifft deshalb mehr als Serverstandorte oder Softwarelizenzen. Sie entscheidet auch darüber, ob Hochschulen ihren eigenen Bildungs- und Wissenschaftsbegriff bewahren. KI kann Informationen aufbereiten, Muster erkennen und Entscheidungen vorbereiten. Die Verantwortung dafür, was richtig, gerecht oder pädagogisch sinnvoll ist, kann sie nicht übernehmen. Souverän ist eine Hochschule daher auch dann, wenn sie technische Möglichkeiten nutzen kann, ohne ihre Urteilskraft an sie abzugeben.

Welche Daten dürfen eine Hochschule verlassen? Welche Systeme gehören zu ihren besonders schützenswerten Bereichen? Lassen sich Inhalte in brauchbaren Formaten exportieren? Was kostet eine spätere Migration? Und kann ein Anbieter gewechselt werden, ohne zentrale Hochschulprozesse neu aufbauen zu müssen? Solche Fragen müssen bereits bei Beschaffung und Systemarchitektur berücksichtigt werden – nicht erst, wenn Preise steigen oder ein Dienst eingestellt wird.

Das KIT reagierte darauf nicht mit einem weiteren Einzeltool, sondern mit einer zentralen KI-Toolbox. Sie verbindet verschiedene Modelle mit gemeinsamen Prompt-Vorlagen, fachbezogenen Chatbots, Teamfunktionen und einem API-Zugang. Ein lokal betriebenes Modell ist als Standard voreingestellt; leistungsfähigere Cloudmodelle müssen bewusst ausgewählt werden. Fast die Hälfte der Anfragen wird dadurch bereits mit dem lokalen Modell bearbeitet.

Souveränität wird hier in die Gestaltung des Angebots eingebaut. Kosten werden sichtbar gemacht, die Nutzung kostenpflichtiger Modelle wird budgetiert und Qualifizierung ist Voraussetzung für den Zugang. Fachabteilungen entwickeln ihre Anwendungen selbst, statt das Thema vollständig an IT oder Datenschutz zu delegieren. Die Hochschule schafft somit nicht nur einen sicheren Zugang zu KI, sondern baut eigenes Erfahrungswissen auf.

Dieser Ansatz gewinnt an Bedeutung, wenn KI-Systeme nicht mehr nur antworten, sondern selbstständig Dateien bearbeiten, Programme aufrufen oder mehrstufige Prozesse ausführen. Mit dem Übergang „von Antwort zu Aktion“ entstehen neue Anforderungen an Berechtigungen, Protokollierung und menschliche Freigaben. Die Frage lautet dann nicht nur, welche KI eine Hochschule anbietet, sondern auch, wie viel Autonomie sie ihr in welchen Prozessen zugesteht.

Bei proprietärer Software werden Pflege und Weiterentwicklung über Lizenzgebühren finanziert. Bei Open Source bleiben diese Kosten oft unsichtbar. Doch auch offene Systeme müssen sicher, barrierefrei und benutzerfreundlich gehalten werden. Das Open Source Development Network in Niedersachsen erprobt deshalb eine gemeinsame Finanzierung von Entwicklungsaufträgen. Der Vergleich aus der Session ist treffend: Hochschulen bauen Forschungsgebäude nicht als kurzfristige Projekte – sie planen und unterhalten sie über Jahre. Kritische Software benötigt eine ähnliche Ressourcenverantwortung.

Digitale Souveränität ist deshalb keine Aufgabe, die jede Hochschule für sich lösen kann. Gemeinsame Infrastrukturen, Entwicklungsfonds und geteiltes Wissen sind keine Ergänzung zur Souveränität, sondern eine ihrer Voraussetzungen.

Gegenüber dem vergangenen Jahr hat sich die Debatte damit spürbar verschoben. 2025 stand vor allem die Gefahr im Mittelpunkt, dass Hochschulen ihre Gestaltungsmacht an kommerzielle Plattformen verlieren. 2026 ging es stärker um die Strukturen, mit denen sie diese Gestaltungsmacht praktisch ausüben können.

Die Diskussion ist zugleich differenzierter geworden. Open Source und Eigenbetrieb bleiben wichtig, aber sie sind keine pauschalen Antworten. Je nach Anwendung kann eine Hochschule selbst entwickeln, gemeinsam betreiben oder Leistungen extern beziehen. Entscheidend ist, dass sie diese Wahl bewusst trifft, kritische Daten und Prozesse kontrolliert und ihre Entscheidung später revidieren kann.

„Under Pressure“ bedeutet in diesem Sinne nicht, möglichst schnell auf jede technologische Entwicklung zu reagieren. Souverän handeln Hochschulen dann, wenn sie unter Druck urteilsfähig bleiben: wenn sie Abhängigkeiten kennen, Alternativen pflegen, Kompetenzen aufbauen und entscheiden können, welchen Zielen ihre digitalen Systeme dienen sollen.

Michael Siegel arbeitet als Kommunikationsmanager beim Hochschulforum Digitalisierung für den Stifterverband. Dort ist er unter anderem mitverantwortlich für Pressearbeit und Online-Redaktion. Zuvor beschäftigte er sich auf vielfältige Weise mit der Kommunikation von Wissenschaft und Forschung und war in der Presse- und Öffentlichkeitsarbeit von Wissenschaft im Dialog tätig, wo er darüber hinaus zahlreiche Diskussionsveranstaltungen organisierte. Er studierte Philosophie, Neuere Deutsche Literatur und Kunstgeschichte an der Philipps-Universität Marburg.
